units.translation: c. smoking with smoke: instead of being smoked; it also means being burned. They are accustomed to smoke fleabane; for its smoke is especially pungent.
138-39a. and the threshing floors: the vine-planted lands. And such are the villages, because in them the sheep and other cattle graze.
c. Lycus, king of the Mariandynians. Lg (P)

140a. and of the Mariandynians: Phineus' children from Cleopatra were Parthenius and Carambis, and from Idaea, daughter of Dardanus, or some Scythian concubine, Thynus and Mariandynus, from whom the peoples are named. Others say that the Mariandynians were named after Mariandynus, son of Cimmerius.
b. their lord being absent: Amycus being absent, that is, clearly dead. The Mariandynians are a people bordering on them.
141. around the iron-bearing land: that of the Chalybes; these are the ones who work iron.
142-43a. and they now the steadings: the Argonauts, when the Bebryces had fled, were plundering the dwellings by the sea; and already having driven off many of the flocks, they were cutting them off.
b. in a circle: turning them around as they drove them to the ship. Lg (P)

145-50a. consider what: the sense: and what would the Bebryces have done, if Heracles had come with us, that is, how would they have fled and been defeated? For I think that there would not even have been a boxing contest, but he would have struck Amycus, who was challenging us with the rules he was laying down, with his club and killed him. L
b. and to be separated instead of to be divided. P
c. 〈to them:〉 the preposition 'with' is missing. Lg
151-53. truly uncared for: the sense: him indeed we left without care—that is, Heracles—and sailed on foreign ships. But with him absent, each of us will perceive how much we have been harmed.
154. 〈all these things:〉 the leaving behind of Heracles. Lg
156. of the wounded: of Iphitus and Talaus. Lg (P)

159-60a. having crowned with laurel: they crowned themselves with laurel for Apollo. They used the crowning in three ways—placing the crowns on the head, on the forehead, on the neck—because the soul is tripartite.

b. and having crowned their blond heads: having crowned their heads above their foreheads with laurel, from which laurel the ropes of the ship were made. Apollonius did not invent the laurel poetically, but there is actually in the place a very large laurel tree, as Androitas of Tenedos says in his Circumnavigation of the Propontis (M. IV 304), noting that the place is called Amycus, and it has settlements even now, and it is five stades distant from the Chalcedonian nymphaeum. Apollodorus in the first book of his Pontica (M. IV 309) says that there is a hero-shrine of Amycus there, and if anyone takes a branch from the laurel, he rises to abuse.
161. well-tuned: melodious; for 'oime' means song. Lg (P)
